overview.title: 📖 Overview: Doubtful Gifts and a Condemned Man's Vow
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 6a–6b
overview.hebrewSource: הַגּוֹסֵס וְהַיּוֹצֵא לֵיהָרֵג — לֹא נִידָּר וְלֹא נֶעֱרָךְ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara first works out when a gentile's donation to the Temple may be accepted — never at the start of construction, and only if unidentifiable as his at the end — and how to handle doubtful intent, as with a gentile's teruma or an inscribed beam, both of which require interment when his purpose is unclear. It then asks whether a coin pledged to charity, or a lamp donated to a synagogue, may still be redirected, distinguishing a Jewish donor from a gentile one. A new mishna turns to a person on his deathbed or condemned to execution: is he the object of a vow, or valuated? The tanna kamma says neither; Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya says he is still valuated, since the Torah's sum is fixed regardless of market value; and Rabbi Yosei holds he can still vow, valuate, and consecrate his own property, and remains liable for damage he causes — a liability the Gemara ties to whether his estate can be made to pay after his execution.

slides.title: 🏛️ Gentile Donations for the Temple — Timing and Type
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan sets out the stages
rows: Nothing accepted, not even water and salt
So the builders do not come to rely on gentiles
Not accepted, since it would be identifiable as his
The cubit-wide spiked plates that keep ravens off the roof
Accepted, since no one could tell it came from him

callout.label: Exception:
callout.text: Nehemiah accepted timber from the Persian king's forest — but government gifts are different, since 'a government does not retract what it says.'

slides.title: 🪙 'This Sela Is for Charity' — Can I Take It Back?
slides.subtitle: Tracking the halakha through several versions

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Naḥman/Rabba bar Avuh: one who pledges a coin to charity may still use it himself and later replace it
2️⃣ Initial understanding: this applies only if he said 'it is incumbent upon me' (a future pledge), not 'THIS coin is for charity' (a specific designation)
3️⃣ Rabbi Yoḥanan (via Rav Ami) and Rava: no such distinction — he may change it in either wording, for himself or for someone else
4️⃣ Final ruling (Rav Zevid of Neharde'a's version): permitted in every combination — but only until the coin reaches the hand of the charity collector; afterward it may no longer be changed

slides.title: 🕯️ Changing a Synagogue Donation — Jew vs. Gentile
slides.subtitle: The same lamp, two very different rules depending on the donor

boxes.title: A Jew's Menorah or Lamp
items: Forbidden to redirect it to a mundane (non-mitzva) use
Permitted to redirect it to a DIFFERENT mitzva

boxes.title: A Gentile's Menorah or Lamp
items: Forbidden to change it at all while his name as donor is still remembered
Permitted once his name has been forgotten
Reason: a gentile donor would protest and demand it back; a Jew would not object to a shift to another mitzva

callout.label: The Sha'azrak story:
callout.text: An Arab merchant donated a lamp to Rav Yehuda's synagogue. It was switched while people might still remember him as the donor — and the Sages disputed among themselves who had acted too hastily.

slides.title: ⚰️ Is a Dying or Condemned Man Vowed About?
slides.subtitle: The mishna's three positions on a goses and one led to execution

lines.speaker: Tanna Kamma
lines.text: Neither a moribund person (גוֹסֵס) nor one being led to execution is the object of a vow, nor is he valuated.

lines.speaker: R' Chanina
lines.text: He IS valuated — his sum is fixed by the Torah according to age and sex, regardless of his actual market value!

lines.speaker: R' Yosei
lines.text: He can still vow to donate another's assessment, take vows of valuation, and consecrate his own property — and if he damages someone else's property, he is liable to pay.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Everyone actually agrees he can vow, valuate, and consecrate. The real dispute with Rabbi Yosei is narrower: only whether he is liable for damage he causes to others.

callout.label: Why 'not vowed about'?
callout.text: A goses has no market value (he cannot be sold); one led to execution likewise has none, and moreover the verse 'anything dedicated shall not be redeemed' (Leviticus 27:29) excludes him once his verdict is issued.

slides.title: 💰 Why Would a Condemned Man's Damage Payment Depend on His Heirs?
slides.subtitle: Tracing the true root of the dispute between the tanna kamma and Rabbi Yosei

nodes.content: ❓ Why does Rabbi Yosei hold one led to execution is liable for damage he causes, while the tanna kamma exempts him?

columns.label: Rav Yosef
columns.content: They dispute whether an ORAL loan can be collected from a debtor's heirs after his death — since he will be executed, only heir-collectible debts remain enforceable

columns.label: Rava
columns.content: Rather, everyone agrees an oral loan is not collectible from heirs; they dispute only whether a Torah-mandated debt (like damages) counts as a 'written' loan that IS collectible from heirs

nodes.content: ✅ Either way, the practical question is the same: can payment be recovered from the condemned man's estate after his execution?

summary.principle: Where a gift's or a vow's true intent is uncertain — a gentile's donation, an unclear consecration, a coin pledged to charity, a lamp given to a synagogue, or the legal status of a dying or condemned man — the Gemara resolves each case by asking precisely what was intended, by whom, and what remains collectible afterward.

flowSteps.content: 🏛️ Gentile Temple gifts accepted only at the end, only if unidentifiable; doubtful teruma/inscriptions require interment
🪙 Charity coin: changeable until it reaches the collector; synagogue lamp: a Jew's may shift mitzvot, a gentile's may not until forgotten

columns.content: ⚰️ Mishna: goses/condemned man not vowed about; R' Chanina — still valuated; R' Yosei — can vow/consecrate, liable for damage
💰 R' Yosei's liability tracks whether a Torah-mandated debt is collectible from the condemned man's estate

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: uncertain intent defaults to caution (interment); a person's legal capacity to obligate himself or his estate is judged precisely, not assumed

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, when may a gentile's donation for Temple maintenance be accepted?
o: At the very beginning of construction, to encourage goodwill
Only at the end of construction, and only if the item cannot be identified as coming from him
Never, under any circumstances
Only if the donation is food, such as water and salt
quiz.e: The Gemara rules that nothing is accepted at the beginning (not even water and salt), and at the end only an unidentifiable, undefined item may be accepted.

quiz.q: Why must a gentile's separated teruma be interred (geniza) when his intent is unclear?
o: Because gentile produce is always forbidden
Because we are concerned his heart may have been directed toward Heaven, i.e., he may have intended to consecrate it rather than give it to a priest
Because teruma may never be separated by a gentile
Because the produce might be diseased
quiz.e: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that without clarity on his intent, the doubtful possibility of a consecration to the Temple requires the produce to be interred rather than used.

quiz.q: Once a coin pledged 'for charity' reaches the hand of the charity collector, what is the rule?
o: It may no longer be exchanged for a different coin
It may always be freely exchanged
It must be doubled before being given
It becomes ownerless property
quiz.e: The baraita states that a coin designated for charity may be changed only before it comes into the possession of the charity collectors; afterward it is fixed.

quiz.q: Why may a gentile's donated synagogue lamp not be redirected to another use, while a Jew's donated lamp may be redirected to a different mitzva?
o: Gentile donations are inherently invalid
A gentile donor would protest and demand its return if he saw it changed, while a Jew would not object to a shift toward another mitzva
Only Jews are permitted to donate synagogue items
Lamps donated by gentiles must always remain lit
quiz.e: The Gemara explains the distinction is behavioral: a gentile donor is expected to protest ('where is the lamp I gave?'), so his gift may not be touched until his name as donor is forgotten.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what does Rabbi Yosei say about one who has been sentenced to execution?
o: He is fully exempt from all halakhic obligations
He can still vow to donate another's assessment, take vows of valuation, and consecrate his own property, and is liable for damage he causes to others
He may no longer own any property at all
He is treated exactly like an ordinary living person in every respect
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei holds that such a person retains the capacity to vow, valuate, and consecrate, and remains liable for damage he causes — a position the Gemara ties to whether such a debt is collectible from his estate.
